title: A brain-inspired name. A governed design.
intro: The prefrontal cortex sits at the front of the brain. It works with other regions to support executive functions: processes that guide behavior toward goals. We use selected functions as design analogies for governed context.
caveat: SOFTWARE ANALOGY · These connections explain our proposed design. They do not reproduce brain biology or prove product performance. Brain regions have overlapping functions. The locations below are approximate. This writing is STE-inspired; full compliance has not been checked.

development.text: Brain development has no single finish date. NIMH describes broad maturation into the mid-to-late 20s. A 2023 study found adult-level performance on its executive-function tasks around 18–20. Task performance and brain structure measure different things. Neither result sets a universal age of maturity. Social context also affects risk-taking.

mappings.fact: Working memory holds information for a current task. Human imaging studies link the dlPFC to maintaining and reorganizing that information. It operates within a wider control network.
mappings.analogy: Keep the current goal, permitted evidence and task state available. The proposed orchestration code limits the context and work budget.
mappings.boundary: A context window is a software resource. It does not reproduce biological working memory or store the whole knowledge base.

mappings.region: Right inferior frontal cortex and connected regions
mappings.fact: Inhibition means stopping a response. Human imaging studies identify a network that includes right inferior frontal cortex, a medial frontal area and a deeper brain region. This network helps slow or stop motor responses.
mappings.analogy: Check permission before retrieval. Stop the request when its scope fails policy. Recheck current records before delivery. Code enforces these gates.
mappings.boundary: Stopping a movement and denying data access are different mechanisms. The analogy explains restraint; it does not establish security.

mappings.fact: Valuation means comparing what options are worth. Human lesion studies link vmPFC to consistent preferences. Other studies connect damage here with emotional changes and difficulties in everyday social behavior.
mappings.analogy: Owners define priorities and acceptable trade-offs. A human reviews the evidence and approves an exact version. Model scores cannot replace that decision authority.
mappings.boundary: Owner-defined rules are explicit software inputs. The product does not gain empathy, emotions or moral judgment from this analogy.
mappings.designTitle: Keep people in charge of priorities

mappings.location: Frontal underside, above the eye sockets
mappings.fact: Human lesion research links the OFC to flexible learning from outcomes. It helps interpret new feedback in the context of earlier outcomes when conditions change.
mappings.analogy: Record outcomes and source changes. Invalidate withdrawn or expired views. Return changed meaning to human review before reuse.
mappings.boundary: A feedback log is not biological learning. Changed meaning still needs approval; a successful output does not make it true.

mappings.location: Front tip of the prefrontal cortex
mappings.fact: A human imaging study linked frontopolar activity to evidence favoring an alternative course of action. The signal tracked the possible benefit of switching from the current choice.
mappings.analogy: Choose an allowed retrieval path: exact ID, hybrid search or approved relationships. Request clarification when evidence is insufficient. Keep every route within the permitted scope.
mappings.boundary: The router follows engineered rules and evaluated signals. This mapping does not claim human planning or an optimal choice.
